caseName: City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd.
court: Supreme Court of the United States
keyFacts: Developer's predecessor sought to develop a 37.6-acre oceanfront parcel in Monterey, virtually surrounded by industrial, commercial, and multifamily uses. The City rejected five successive development proposals over several years, imposing progressively more stringent demands each time. The developer sued under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983 alleging the pattern of rejections effected a regulatory taking without compensation and violated due process/equal protection.
outcome: The case was tried to a jury, which found for the developer on the takings theory and awarded damages. The Ninth Circuit and, in a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court affirmed both the jury's verdict and its authority to decide the takings-liability question -- a first for a regulatory-takings damages suit.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury damages verdict for the regulatory taking, affirmed through the Supreme Court
notes: Landmark case establishing that a regulatory-taking liability question in a Section 1983 damages suit is triable to a jury. The rejected proposals evolved through both residential and visitor-serving/commercial concepts, so it is not a purely residential dispute even though it is most often cited as a takings case.

keyFacts: Developer acquired 34 acres for roughly $3 million to construct a 184,000-square-foot industrial/commercial building, obtained site plan approval and a building permit, and spent more than $4 million on land and construction. The Town then revoked the permit and amended its Zoning Code to preclude commercial buildings on the parcel, halting the project.
outcome: The Court of Appeals affirmed reinstatement of the building permit and a damages award to the developer for the Town's Section 1983 violation of the developer's vested property rights, plus costs and attorneys' fees.
dollarAmountBasis: Trial court damages award for losses flowing from the wrongful permit revocation, affirmed on appeal, plus costs and attorneys' fees
notes: One of the largest disclosed Section 1983 zoning-damages awards in this dataset involving a commercial/industrial building. Established New York's two-part vested-rights test for substantive due process zoning claims (requires a vested property interest and either an entitlement or a bad-faith abuse of process).

caseName: Mammoth Lakes Land Acquisition, LLC v. Town of Mammoth Lakes
court: California Court of Appeal, Third Appellate District
keyFacts: The Town entered a development agreement obligating it to process the developer's airport-area hotel/condominium project and to exercise discretionary approvals reasonably, in good faith, and in a timely manner. The Town instead effectively stalled the project for years, citing unresolved FAA airport-expansion/funding issues not expressly tied to the agreement's conformance requirements.
outcome: A jury found the Town breached the development agreement. The trial court entered judgment for the developer, and the Court of Appeal affirmed both the compensatory damages award and a separate attorney-fee award, rejecting the Town's exhaustion and performance-excuse defenses.
dollarAmountBasis: Jury verdict for breach-of-development-agreement damages, affirmed on appeal (plus a separate attorney-fee award of approximately $2.3 million, also affirmed)
notes: The judgment (roughly $32.3M with fees) forced the Town of Mammoth Lakes into a Chapter 9 municipal bankruptcy filing shortly after. This research did not independently verify the town's final total payout after the bankruptcy proceedings, so the figure recorded here is the appellate-affirmed jury award, not necessarily the final cash amount collected.

caseName: City Heights Holdings LLC v. City of Cle Elum
citation: Arbitration award (Hon. Paris Kallas, ret., arbitrator), November 2024; related confirmation proceedings in King County Superior Court
court: Contractual arbitration under the parties' development agreement, with related King County Superior Court proceedings
keyFacts: City Heights Holdings (developer Sean Northrop) and the City of Cle Elum signed a 25-year development agreement in 2011 for the roughly 1,000-home Ederra project on 350+ acres. When the developer sought subdivision permits in late 2019, the City required a full discretionary planning process instead of the streamlined 45-day administrative review the agreement had promised.
outcome: The arbitrator ruled the City breached the 2011 development agreement and assessed damages against the City several times larger than the City's entire annual general fund, prompting the City Council to vote 5-2 in January 2025 to pursue Chapter 9 municipal bankruptcy -- the first in Washington State since 1991.
dollarAmountBasis: Arbitration damages award for breach of the 2011 development agreement's discretionary-approval-timing covenant
notes: Resolved by contractual arbitration rather than a court judgment, but is a real, extensively reported dollar outcome showing the scale of municipal exposure when a development agreement's approval-timing covenant is breached. The underlying Ederra project was primarily residential; included because the development-agreement breach mechanics and damages exposure are directly transferable to commercial development agreements, and because comparably well-documented commercial-only development-agreement judgments of this size were not found in the time available.

caseName: Township of Salem v. Miller Penn Development LLC
keyFacts: Under a Township-approved subdivision development agreement, a developer built a subdivision street (Shaw Court) that did not comply with required layering/compaction specifications and constructed the cul-de-sac at roughly 60 feet in diameter instead of the required 80 feet; the developer never posted the required improvement-completion security.
outcome: The Commonwealth Court affirmed a judgment for the Township against the developer for the cost of remedying the defective public improvements, rejecting both the Township's larger, more speculative damages claim and the developer's statute-of-limitations defense under the nullum tempus doctrine (limitations periods do not run against a government enforcing public rights).
dollarAmountBasis: Court-awarded cost-to-repair damages ($8,265.95 to resurface deteriorated pavement plus $17,322.50 to reconstruct the undersized cul-de-sac), affirmed on appeal
notes: Illustrates the reverse fact pattern in this claim type -- a municipality successfully suing a developer for breach of a subdivision/development-improvement agreement -- useful for benchmarking the much smaller typical dollar scale of these municipality-as-plaintiff disputes against the developer-as-plaintiff cases in this dataset.

caseName: Allen Distribution v. West Pennsboro Township Zoning Hearing Board
keyFacts: A prospective purchaser/developer sought and obtained two Township ordinances rezoning 133 acres from high-density residential to industrial in order to construct industrial/warehouse buildings. Neighboring property owners challenged the rezoning as illegal spot zoning benefiting a single landowner without a reasonable planning basis.
outcome: The zoning hearing board found, and the Court of Common Pleas and Commonwealth Court affirmed, that the rezoning constituted invalid spot zoning; the rezoning ordinances were struck down and the industrial development could not proceed under that zoning.
notes: Purely declaratory/injunctive outcome -- no damages were sought or awarded. Illustrates that successful spot-zoning challenges typically come from neighboring objectors defeating a developer's favorable rezoning, not from the developer's own affirmative claim.

caseName: Lathan v. Union County Board of Commissioners
keyFacts: Union County rezoned an 11.4-acre parcel from residential to light-industrial use despite the county's own growth-management plan providing that industrial development should not diminish the desirability of surrounding residential uses.
outcome: The Court of Appeals held, as a matter of law, that the rezoning constituted invalid spot zoning and invalidated the ordinance.
notes: Older but still frequently cited North Carolina spot-zoning precedent. Purely declaratory relief (ordinance invalidated); no damages claim was involved.

caseName: Chaffier v. Hellertown Borough Zoning Hearing Board
citation: No. 907 C.D. 2022 (Pa. Commw. Ct. Jan. 10, 2024) (unpublished memorandum opinion)
keyFacts: Borough Council rezoned a single parcel from R-1 to R-2 in early 2020 at the property owner's request. The parcel became the only R-2-zoned land east of Easton Road, prompting a neighbor's challenge that the rezoning was invalid spot zoning benefiting one landowner without a comprehensive planning rationale.
outcome: The Commonwealth Court struck down the rezoning ordinance as illegal spot zoning.
notes: Recent (2024) example showing spot-zoning challenges remain a live and successful cause of action for neighboring objectors. Purely injunctive/declaratory outcome; unpublished opinion, so persuasive rather than binding precedent.

caseName: Sam Commercial Properties LLC v. Town of Mooresville
keyFacts: Petitioner applied in 2021 for a permit to erect a digital billboard within Mooresville's commercially-zoned Highway 150/I-77 corridor. The Town's planning director denied the application, and the Board of Adjustment affirmed, interpreting the Town's ordinance to generally prohibit billboards except limited Highway Beautification Act-compliant signs.
outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed, holding the Board misinterpreted the ordinance and that ambiguity in a billboard-permitting ordinance must be resolved in favor of the free use of property; the court remanded with instructions that the permit be issued.
notes: Purely injunctive/declaratory outcome (permit ordered issued); no damages were claimed. Representative of the routine, non-constitutional variance/permit-appeal track that operates separately from Section 1983 claims.

caseName: Matter of Franklin Sq. Realty Assoc., LLC v. Board of Appeals of the Town of Hempstead
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Second Department
keyFacts: Owner of a split-zoned (business/residence) parcel in Franklin Square applied in 2021 for a building permit to construct a self-storage facility with a parking lot. The Buildings Department denied the application on the ground that use variances were required, and the Board of Appeals affirmed the denial.
outcome: The Appellate Division upheld the Board's determination as having a rational basis and not being arbitrary and capricious, denying the petitioner's Article 78 challenge to the permit denial.
notes: Plaintiff/developer LOST -- the permit denial was affirmed, not overturned. Included specifically to document the more common losing outcome in routine variance-denial appeals, where courts generally defer to zoning boards absent a rational-basis failure.

caseName: Lockaway Storage v. County of Alameda
court: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District
keyFacts: Lockaway received a three-year permit in 1999 to build a self-storage facility in Castro Valley. When the permit lapsed before construction began, the County refused to grant an extension based on an erroneous application of Measure D, a voter-approved growth-control initiative, causing roughly a decade of delay before Lockaway could ultimately build.
outcome: The Court of Appeal affirmed a damages award against the County for the temporary regulatory-taking effect of its erroneous permit-extension denial, plus attorney's fees; the California Supreme Court denied the County's petition for review (6-0), leaving the award intact.
dollarAmountBasis: Combined damages and attorney-fee award for the County's erroneous, years-long permit-extension denial, affirmed on appeal and left standing by the California Supreme Court's denial of review
notes: One of the few cases in this dataset combining a permit-denial appeal with a disclosed, sizable damages recovery for the delay itself, rather than purely prospective relief.

caseName: The Smoking Tree LLC (Jacob Schlichter) v. City of Albert Lea
citation: Minnesota Court of Appeals, decided May 18, 2026 (unpublished)
keyFacts: Schlichter obtained the state's first cannabis microbusiness license from the Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management in July 2025 and applied the same day for the City of Albert Lea's local business registration required to operate. The City Council voted to deny the registration.
outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed, holding the City Council's denial violated its own ordinance and was arbitrary and made without reason, and remanded for the City to reconsider the application under the correct standard.
notes: Very recent (2026) example of a local business/use-permit denial appeal succeeding on judicial review. Purely declaratory relief (remand for reconsideration); no damages awarded. Cannabis-use permitting has become a high-volume source of commercial zoning-denial litigation nationally.

caseName: Avenue 6E Investments, LLC v. City of Yuma
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
keyFacts: Two developers sought rezoning to permit higher-density housing on their parcel. The City Council denied the request -- its only denial out of 76 rezoning applications over the prior three years, and contrary to its own planning staff's recommendation -- amid what the court characterized as racially charged public opposition invoking Hispanic residents.
outcome: The Ninth Circuit reversed dismissal and summary judgment that had been entered for the City, holding the developers stated plausible Equal Protection Clause and Fair Housing Act disparate-treatment claims, and remanded for trial. A publicly reported final damages figure or settlement amount from the remand was not located in this research pass.
notes: Landmark Ninth Circuit case establishing that racially motivated zoning/rezoning denials are actionable under equal protection and the FHA even at the pleading stage. Flagged for follow-up with paid docket/verdict database access to confirm the ultimate remand outcome.

caseName: Nasierowski Bros. Investment Co. v. City of Sterling Heights
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
keyFacts: A developer conditioned its purchase of land on the City's assurance that the parcel could be developed for commercial retail/warehouse use. A City councilman living near the property proposed a zoning amendment that was adopted without notice or a hearing, specifically eliminating the developer's intended commercial use for that parcel.
outcome: The Sixth Circuit held that the City's failure to provide notice or a hearing before rezoning the specific parcel violated procedural due process, reversed summary judgment for the City, and remanded for further proceedings. A final damages figure from the remand was not identified in this research pass.
notes: Frequently cited for the principle that a procedural due process zoning claim is ripe for federal court without exhausting state remedies, unlike substantive due process/takings claims which generally require a final decision and exhaustion.

court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
keyFacts: A developer sought a permit for a residential/tourist development in Loiza, Puerto Rico. Permit processing was delayed roughly five years, which the developer alleged was the product of political favoritism and bad-faith administrative conduct, and sued under Section 1983 for the resulting delay damages.
outcome: The First Circuit rejected the developer's substantive due process claim, holding that a bad-faith failure to follow state administrative procedures does not amount to a federal due process deprivation where adequate state-court review is available. The plaintiff lost on the constitutional claim.
notes: Foundational First Circuit precedent rejecting substantive due process claims premised on permit-processing delay. Illustrates the high bar (conscience-shocking conduct, no adequate state remedy) that most Section 1983 zoning-delay claims fail to clear.

court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
keyFacts: Developer Steven Sherman paid $2.7 million for land intending a residential subdivision and alleged the Town spent years stringing him along with shifting demands rather than approving or denying his application outright, ultimately causing him to spend roughly $5.5 million attempting to comply.
outcome: The Second Circuit vacated dismissal of Sherman's substantive due process and equal protection claims as unripe, allowing the suit to proceed past the pleading stage. On remand, the district court dismissed the substantive due process, equal protection, and state-law claims on the merits in March 2015 -- the plaintiff ultimately did not recover on the federal claims.
notes: Illustrates a common pattern: an initial appellate win on ripeness/procedural grounds followed by an ultimate loss once the substantive claim is actually litigated. The same underlying dispute later produced the U.S. Supreme Court's 2017 intervention-standing decision, Town of Chester v. Laroe Estates, Inc., 137 S. Ct. 1645 (2017), involving a later-intervening developer.

caseName: Green Genie, Inc. v. City of Detroit
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
keyFacts: Green Genie sought a medical marijuana dispensary permit for a location the City determined was within 1,000 feet of a school, inside Detroit's ordinance-defined drug-free zone. The company sued alleging the denial violated substantive due process and equal protection, pointing to other facilities it claimed were treated more favorably.
outcome: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, holding Green Genie failed to identify valid similarly-situated comparators and that the City had denied numerous other applicants for the same drug-free-zone reason. The plaintiff lost.
notes: Cannabis-use permitting has become one of the more common recent sources of Section 1983 zoning/licensing litigation. This case shows the routine losing outcome when a plaintiff cannot show discriminatory intent or a valid comparator.

caseName: Rubicon Real Estate Holdings, LLC v. City of Pontiac
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
keyFacts: Developer sought to redevelop the Glenwood Plaza property in Pontiac for mixed-use purposes including medical marijuana cultivation/processing. Roughly two years of delay (2019-2021) in obtaining zoning approvals and licensing caused prospective tenants to withdraw and the project to collapse, allegedly worsened by a city official's interference with the developer's other business relationships.
outcome: The district court granted summary judgment for the City; the Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding the developer lacked a constitutionally protected property interest in discretionary permits and that the bureaucratic delay, however frustrating, was not 'extraordinary' enough to constitute a taking or a due process violation.
notes: Very recent (2026) confirmation that discretionary-permit delay claims, even where a project collapses and tenants withdraw as a result, routinely fail as a matter of law absent a protected property interest -- the plaintiff recovered nothing.
